en.headline: From OA to Security — A Trajectory Built on One Conviction
paragraphs: My career started inside Korea Aerospace Industries' closed network, tracking patch schedules for the closed-network Linux fleet on an Excel sheet. Repeating the same operations every week led to one conviction: the value of security operations is not hoping incidents never happen, but lowering risk through repeatable procedures and runbooks. I then consecutively earned RHCSA, LPIC-1, and Linux Master Level 2 to rebuild my Linux foundation, and carried that base into hands-on operations.

At Metanet M Platform I picked up Ansible and Python, automating the NAC policy deployment procedure for a large-scale contact center. At Jointree, I applied NSX-T microsegmentation to Kookmin University's next-generation information system, reducing east-west traffic blind spots and reorganizing the NAC and DLP detection policies. The tools changed, but the principle didn't: any task that repeatedly takes manual effort is a candidate for runbooks.

At Quantec Investment Management's Financial Security Data Center (FSDC), responding to Financial Supervisory Service audits taught me that security operations is not about setting things up once, but about being able to present operational evidence with data during audits and incidents. Tuning DB access-control queries and validating a PB platform POC were both about explaining the operational state with data and leaving a trail behind every change.

Most recently, in the Nextrade exchange security track, I was engaged continuously from build (Gaonnuri) through operations (ITCEN CTS). I built and operated network segmentation and endpoint security controls, passed the FSC main-license review, standardized security appliance configuration with Ansible Role, and connected Splunk ES detection rules, alert workflow notifications, and FortiManager API policy lookups to standardize the recognition, classification, and alerting flow for security events.

Next, I am widening the scope of operational tooling from security appliances and scripts toward MCP and Edge runtimes. My homelab — Cloudflare Workers, MCP, Grafana, 1Password — runs on Terraform-managed IaC where I experiment with patterns in which an MCP tool makes the first pass over repetitive security-operations items. In my next chapter, I want the operational problem to come before the tool, and to take on the role of turning that problem into a repeatable operating structure.
en.closing: I will carry this trajectory — built on a single question about the limits of repetitive work — into the next problem your security infrastructure needs to solve, and answer it the same way.
